title: London System: how Black fights it
outcomes: Names three replies to 2.Bf4 (strike with the c-pawn, build with the e-pawn, mirror with the light bishop) and what each asks of Black
Counts attackers and defenders of d4 before capturing, and explains what a bishop on g4 adds (a pin on the knight)
Decides whether a queen trip to b6 is safe by listing who defends d5 once the queen leaves
Puts the light bishop outside the pawn chain before the e-pawn moves, and says why
Compares a trade offered by a knight on h5 with the engine's other bishop moves

steps.caption: Black to move after 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4. White's bishop is already outside the pawn chain and nothing defends it yet. Black has three families of answer: strike at d4 with the c-pawn, build solidly with a pawn on e6, or bring out the light bishop first. Look at the position and decide which you would try, and what you would count before you commit.

claims.statement: Nothing of White's defends the bishop on f4 yet.
Nothing of Black's attacks the bishop on f4 yet.

steps.text: **What you can do after this lesson.** After 2.Bf4 Black has several sound moves, so the skill is not memorising one. It is knowing what each reply asks you to count, which piece to place first, and which tempting queen move to skip. In our masters data (329,379 games, both players 2500 or more) Black chose the knight move ...Nf6 in 562 games, which keeps all three plans open, and the pawn strike ...c5 in 371 [V]. Small samples: they show taste, not proof.

steps.caption: Reply one: attack the centre at once. Step through the plan. After each move, count how many pieces attack d4 and how many defend it.

line.say: The pawn attacks d4 at once. Only the queen defends it, so White must respond.
A pawn now defends d4. It also guards the bishop on f4.
A second attacker joins the pawn on d4.
A third defender arrives. Two attackers face three defenders.

claims.statement: After ...c5 the pawn attacks d4.
After ...c5 only the queen defends d4.
After e3 the queen and the e-pawn defend d4.
After ...Nc6 two Black pieces attack d4.
After Nf3 three White pieces defend d4.

steps.caption: The pin. White to move after 3...Nc6. Step through the developing move and the bishop that answers it.

line.say: White develops and defends d4 a third time. This is the position you just counted.
The bishop attacks the knight, and the queen stands behind it. If the knight moves, the queen is next.
White backs up d4 with a pawn. The knight on f3 is still pinned.

claims.statement: The bishop on g4 attacks the knight on f3.
The queen still stands on d1, behind the knight.
At depth 16 the position after ...Bg4 is within 0.3 pawn of equal.
After White's c3 the bishop on g4 still attacks the knight on f3.

steps.text: **Count, then decide.** Two attackers against three defenders: taking on d4 would not win a pawn. The point of ...Bg4 is different: it pins the knight on f3 to the queen, so White usually answers with c3, Nbd2 or a bishop move. [I] A pinned defender counts for less than it looks. Pressure makes the opponent answer; it does not win material.

**The queen hits two pawns.** After the pawn strike and White's e3, the queen move to b6 attacks the pawn on b2 and backs up the pawn on c5, so it looks forcing. Before you play a move like that, ask what the piece stopped doing when it left its square. Here, the queen leaves d8. Step through the idea, then predict three positions.

steps.caption: Black to move after 3.e3. Step through the queen sortie and the natural reply.

line.say: The queen attacks b2 and backs up the pawn on c5. She also stops guarding d5.
White develops with a threat: the knight attacks d5, and nothing defends it.

claims.statement: The queen on b6 attacks b2 and defends c5.
After Nc3 the knight attacks d5.
After ...Qb6 nothing of Black's defends d5.
After Nc3 the pawn on d5 is loose (attacked, undefended).
At depth 16 the position after Nc3 is rated 0.4 to 1.5 pawns better for White.

steps.title: One defender decides it
steps.prompt: In all three positions Black has just played the queen to b6 and it is White's move. Predict for each whether the engine rates the position within 0.5 pawn of equal, then check. The second has no knight on f6 guarding d5 (a spare pawn move on h6 stands in for it). The third adds h3 and ...h6 to the first.

steps.text: **When the queen trip is safe.** In the failing position only the queen guarded d5, so once she left, Nc3 won a tempo. In the working one the knight on f6 kept guarding d5, so nothing was loose. [I] Before you move a piece, check who else guards what it guards; if nobody does, you need a concrete reason.

steps.caption: Reply two, the solid one. Before the pawn goes to e6, the bishop on c8 can go to five squares. Step through the pawn move and count again.

line.say: The pawn opens the diagonal of the f8 bishop. It shuts the c8 bishop in behind it.

claims.statement: Before the pawn move the bishop on c8 can go to five squares.
After the pawn move the bishop on c8 can go to one square.

steps.caption: The same pawn move after the bishop has come out. Step through and watch the bishop on f5.

line.say: The bishop develops before the e-pawn can lock it in. It mirrors White's bishop on f4.
White develops and opens the way for the bishop on f1.
Now the pawn can go to e6: the bishop on f5 is outside the chain. White will develop a knight and Black will answer with ...Nf6.

claims.statement: From f5 the bishop attacks the pawn on c2.
After the pawn move to e6 the bishop on f5 still has legal moves.

steps.text: **The bishop comes first.** Black's light bishop is the piece that the e-pawn shuts in, so the order matters: bishop out, then the pawn. The price is that the bishop on f5 can be hit by tempo moves, and White's c-pawn can strike at d5. [H] A bishop developed outside the pawn chain is the Black version of White's own bishop on f4, which is why the structures mirror each other. Test it in the next position.

steps.caption: Challenging the bishop with a knight. Black to move. Step through the offer of a trade and count what each side gets.

line.say: The knight attacks the bishop. The pawn on e3 defends it, so Black is offering a trade.
White keeps the bishop for the moment.
Black trades the knight for the bishop. White will retake with the h-pawn, which puts the rook on h1 behind a half-open h-file.

claims.statement: After ...Nh5 the knight attacks the bishop on f4.
The pawn on e3 defends the bishop on f4.
After the trade only Black owns two bishops.
After hxg3 the h-file is half open for White.

steps.text: **What the trade does.** Black wins the pair of bishops; White gets a half-open h-file and a pawn on g3. Neither side is clearly better. But the engine prefers other bishop moves, shown next. [H] The trade is a practical decision: it removes the piece that defines White's setup, at the price of giving the two bishops away. Decide whether you want that before you offer it.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine a beginner who plays Black against the London System. In your own words, write four short answers.

fields.label: The idea: what Black's three replies ask for
When the queen trip to b6 works, and when it does not
One example a beginner could set up on a board

steps.text: **Self-check.** Two concrete checks, both yours. First: name the piece that defends d5 after ...Qb6 in each of the three positions you predicted. Second: say which move must come before ...e6, and why. If either answer is hazy, go back to the matching board. Nothing here is graded.

**Recap.** [1] After 2.Bf4 Black has several sound replies. [2] The c-pawn and a knight add attackers on d4, but count before capturing. [3] A bishop on g4 ties a knight to its queen. [4] Before a queen trip, check who else guards the pawn she leaves. [5] Put the light bishop out before the e-pawn moves. [6] A knight on h5 offers a trade; compare it with moving the bishop. [7] Checked: engine claims at depth 16 and attacker counts.
